newsitem.title: USA: US gasoline prices take holiday jump at pump - AAA.
newsitem.headline: US gasoline prices take holiday jump at pump - AAA.

text.p: Retail gasoline prices, defying typical seasonal trends of falling during autumn and winter, are instead moving up amid the lowest stocks in a generation, the American Automobile Association (AAA) said.

The AAA survey showed the average price this December of regular unleaded self-serve gasoline of nearly $1.29 a gallon -- 17 cents above year-ago levels, a cent higher than in November and just a touch below highs hit last summer.
"As long as refiners have lower inventories, we're going to see price spikes," said Mike Morrissey, a spokesman with AAA in Florida.

U.S. oil refiners have moved in the last year to minimize stocks of all hydrocarbons, including crude oil, heating oil and gasoline to free working capital in an industry pressured in recent years by poor profit margins.
But, consumer groups, including AAA, counter that motorists will invariably have to pay higher prices since the supply-demand balance is more delicate when stocks are low.
"Higher prices are not the kind of news you want just before Christmas," said William Berman, an AAA official in Washington, D.C. "Refiners are gambling with us, the motoring public," he said.
In the last month, prices have risen the most in the Great Lakes region by $0.027 to $1.309, followed by New England, where prices rose by $0.015 to $1.308 a gallon.
Prices were highest in the West, though they actually slipped in the last month by $0.003 to $1.363 a gallon.

According to the American Petroleum Institute, an industry trade group, gasoline stocks are now below 200 million barrels -- a critical threshold below which many industry analysts consider prices more vulnernable to price spikes.
Both Berman and Morrissey said U.S. motorists are increasingly puzzled and angry over the way gasoline prices are again near summer highs.
"Americans have come to expect cheaper gasoline, and when prices go up, they look for someone to blame," Morrissey said.
Some industry sources reckon prices may be coming down in the coming weeks as Iraqi crude again flows on international markets for the first time since it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
But sources like Morrissey warned motorists should not hold their breaths since prices typically rise faster than they fall.
